articles.text: This summer, a group of young soccer players from Piedmont traveled to Sweden and Denmark to compete in two of the world’s largest and most respected international youth soccer tournaments: the Gothia Cup and the Dana Cup. The local players included Eloise McDowell (PSC GP U12), Pierce McDowell (PSC BP U12), Kate Nealon (AFC), Josh Nealon (LAMO), Lola Ruthven (AFC), Kellan Ruthven (PSC BP U12), Ramsey Stull (PSC BP U12), and Troy Wallway (PSC BP U12). The players represented National Soccer Academy (NSA), an organization that has brought teams to these prestigious tournaments for 35 years. The trip gave the Piedmont athletes an opportunity to compete internationally, experience Scandinavian culture, and build friendships with players from around the world. The Gothia Cup, held annually in Gothenburg, Sweden, began in 1975 and has grown into the world’s largest and most international youth soccer tournament. In a typical year, approximately 1,900 teams from about 75 countries compete in nearly 5,000 matches played on more than 100 fields throughout Gothenburg. One of the tournament’s highlights is its opening ceremony, during which thousands of players enter the stadium wearing their club uniforms and carrying their national flags. The celebration creates an atmosphere similar to a major professional sporting event. Although the level of competition is high, the Gothia Cup is about more than winning. Its broader mission is to bring young people together regardless of nationality, religion, or background, using soccer as a shared language. Following the Gothia Cup, the players traveled to Hjørring, Denmark, for the Dana Cup. Founded in 1982, the Dana Cup is Denmark’s largest sporting event and one of the world’s leading youth soccer tournaments. Each summer, it welcomes approximately 1,000 teams and 20,000 players and participants, along with thousands of supporters, referees, and volunteers. Teams from around 56 countries take part. The Dana Cup begins with an opening procession through the streets of Hjørring. Players march together wearing their club colors and carrying flags before entering the stadium. The tournament offers age divisions for both boys and girls and is known for its international atmosphere, well-organized matches, quality fields, and emphasis on equality, friendship, respect, and unity. Competing against teams from different countries introduced the Piedmont players to a variety of playing styles. Some opponents relied on speed and physical play, while others emphasized technical ability, possession, and quick passing. The experience challenged the players to adjust their strategies, communicate effectively, work together, and remain confident under pressure. The benefits of the trip also extended beyond the soccer field. Traveling internationally with a team encouraged responsibility, independence, time management, and respect for other cultures. For the Piedmont players, the Gothia Cup and Dana Cup were much more than ordinary soccer tournaments. The experience gave them a chance to test their abilities at a high level, represent their local clubs and community, and create friendships and memories that may last a lifetime.

articles.text: Caltrans has published its findings on the potential effects of lifting the truck ban on Highway I-580. The study indicates that there would be no benefits for residents in East or West Oakland in terms of a healthier environment. However, it highlights significant advantages for the freight industry. Caltrans has released a feedback survey for residents to voice their opinions. It can be found at the following link: https://www.surveymonkey. com/r/i580TAS-Survey. According to the 2025 WOCAP Report. Heavy and medium-duty trucks on I-880 contribute the least PM 2.5, at levels the EPA does not consider harmful. Local streets and industrial sites account for most pollution, as does road dust. Whether trucks use 880 or both freeways will not change ‘local’ conditions. Truck Volumes The Study estimates that if the truck ban were lifted today, we would see some 4,400 trucks per day on I-580. Over a 16-hour day (6 a.m.- 6 p.m. is when most truck travel occurs), that amounts to one truck every 13 seconds. State Route 13 (the Warren Freeway) would see 900 trucks (compared to 400 now). Tunnel Road would expect 270 heavy trucks; Hesperian, Hegenberger and 150th would each see 400+ trucks each day. Other arterials such as High St, Park, 14th Avenue and Fruitvale were not deemed significant but, as the study team acknowledged, the model-assessed impacts may not be reality. Even a small number of additional trucks on some of these streets may have outsized impacts. Ashby Avenue could expect 190 additional trucks and Grand Ave about 140 more trucks between Harrison and MacArthur Blvd. Speed Lifting the truck ban on I-580 would result in higher speeds for trucks on all freeways in the network. Some 67% could travel at speeds of over 60mph (only 49% can do so with the ban). The commercial speed limit on California highways is 55mph. The study noted truckers would need to ‘be more careful’ in tighter turns while driving on 580s on and off ramps. The study flagged this: “Increasing the number of trucks traveling at speeds greater than 55mph…could increase the severity of truck-involved collisions…” It also acknowledged speeds on local streets could increase, which presents a challenge to ‘determine how changes in truck speeds could impact collision severity. Air Quality The Study’s fundamental premise was to evaluate potential improvements in air quality in East and West Oakland, with a focus on improved health outcomes. The finding that lifting the ban on I-580 would not improve health outcomes for these communities is relevant. Exposure to Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5, a measure of air quality, shows that the Study Area as a whole has equivalent exposure. Structural Capacity The Study’s assertion that I-580 is structurally capable of handling heavy-duty trucks was based on the overhead clearances being sufficient and on its use by buses. The 100 or so buses that use I-580 daily weigh 45- 54 pounds. This is not equivalent to thousands of trucks weighing up to 80,000 pounds. Highway 880 was built in the late 1950s specifically as the region’s freight corridor. The Port, Airport, and Oakland-San Leandro-Hayward area industrial hubs evolved in tandem. Highway 880 is maintained as a ‘state of the art’ freight corridor. Highway 580, built just a few years later, 1) replaced the segment of MacArthur Blvd that previously served as Highway 50, and 2) was designated as a ‘Scenic Highway’ and NOT for trucks. One of the agreements was to honor the 1951 truck ban between Grand Ave and San Leandro. The Study’s assertions about the number of trucks on both highways with and without the ban, today and in 2035, use a dated traffic model. It also ignores disincentives that providing new capacity promulgates. For example: • The Port’s freight tonnage today is 15-20% lower than in 2016, but the number of heavyduty trucks serving the Port increased 5-10%. • The trucking industry structurally adapts to increased capacity, and the trend is for smaller, more frequent deliveries with more trucks. The fundamentals of road congestion law and economics tell us industry scales operations to capacity. • Carriers that currently move goods at night will shift to daytime hours • More road capacity disadvantages rail and other clean strategies, economically Implying lifting the truck ban on I-580 will improve health in East and West Oakland is inaccurate and misleading. Lifting the truck ban on I-580 will not change the number of trucks or the most congested parts. Conditions will worsen for 580 while 880 will see minor improvements. Only the freight industry wins. Several elected officials have taken a stand against lifting the ban. The “No Big Rigs” organization hopes to get all the area State senators, assembly representatives, County and local officials to do the same.

articles.text: On Wednesday, August 12 Piedmont School Board held its first regularly scheduled meeting of the school year. The meeting’s headline event was the official naming of Donald Evans as interim superintendent. Changes to the faculty were noted and Facilities Director Pete Palmer gave a summary of projects completed over the summer. The meeting began with a new speaker. articles.text: Dr. Donald Evans was welcomed back to Piedmont and confirmed as the interim school superintendent during the first school board meeting of the year, on August 12. Evans was on hand to symbolically take the torch from Jennifer Hawn and begin his second one-year term guiding the school district. “There are so many emotions going through my mind right now. I feel so good about being here, this is my family,“ said Evans. Board President Ruchi Medhekar called the approval of Evans a full circle moment, and characterized the work with Evans as “joyful and full of laughter.” “[Evans has] deep expertise, and a true understanding of this community and what this community needs,” said Medhekar. The return of Evans received the stamp of approval from Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) Co-President Elise Marks as well. “Dr. Donald Evans, who we know from a very happy experience in 2022-23, is an incredibly steady hand at the wheel as we navigate this time of transition. It’s a huge relief to have him joining us again. We are eager to get back to work together,” said Marks. Board member Lindsay Thomasson called Evans’ arrival “the silver lining” to Supt. Jennifer Hawn’s quick departure. Both Thomasson and Medhekar started their board of education tenures at the start of 2023 when Evans was at the helm of the district. “You came to Piedmont four years ago when the district was on extremely shaky ground. I’m happy to share that you are now walking into a much stronger and more stable district,” said Thomasson. “This is a special place and so having the opportunity to come back and continue your [Hawn’s] work and the board’s vision and mission for this district and to work with all of you again, means so much to me,” said Evans. She stated that the board interviewed two other candidates for the Interim Superintendent in the two weeks following Hawn’s announcement. “I’m excited and joyful, I’ll add a little bit of heart to that joy and try to mix it up and create this amazing environment that you already have here,” said Evans.

articles.text: On Saturday, September 26, from 6:30 to 9:15 p.m., community members will have a unique opportunity to explore that question with some of the people working at the forefront of artificial intelligence. “AI: Will It Save or End the World?” will take place at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School and will feature a screening of the acclaimed 2026 documentary The AI Doc, followed by a live panel discussion and audience Q&A. The panel brings together four technology and media leaders: • Jeff Bleich: The Chief Legal Officer at Anthropic, brings a perspective from one of the world’s leading AI companies and from his extensive experience in law, government, and technology. • Marco Casalaina: VP Products, Core AI and AI Futurist at Microsoft, leads Microsoft’s AI Futures team, which identifies emerging AI trends and develops products for the next generation of artificial intelligence. He previously led teams across Azure AI, including Azure OpenAI, Responsible AI and AI Studio. • Clara Shih: founder of New Work Foundation and advisor to Meta Business AI, is the former CEO of Salesforce AI and a TIME100 AI honoree. • Emily Chang: host and executive producer at Bloomberg Media and one of the country’s best-known technology journalists, will moderate the discussion. The evening is intended not as a technical seminar, but as a community conversation about questions increasingly confronting families, students, educators and businesses. Is AI developing too quickly? How will it change education and the careers today’s students are preparing for? Which jobs will disappear, which will be transformed, and which new ones will emerge? Can increasingly powerful AI systems be trusted? And how can society capture the enormous potential benefits of AI while managing its risks? Those questions may be especially relevant for high school students, who are encouraged to attend, as the film and panel will address how AI could affect university choices, careers and the skills young people will need in a rapidly changing economy. The program will begin with a screening of The AI Doc, which examines the opportunities and dangers presented by artificial intelligence. Following the film, Chang will lead the panelists in a discussion before opening the conversation to questions directly from the audience. For a community located just a few miles from the center of the AI revolution, the subject is particularly close to home. Whether you believe artificial intelligence will usher in an era of unprecedented innovation, worry that the technology is advancing faster than society can manage, or simply want to understand what all the excitement is about, the evening offers Piedmont residents a chance to hear directly from people helping shape AI’s future. Sponsored by Piedmont Unified Schools, Piedmont Parents Network, and Piedmont Makers, tickets are available with a $50 donation per person, with all proceeds going to Piedmont Boosters and PUSD. Learn more and buy tickets at: https://piedmontstore.org/products/ai-will-it-save-or-end-theworld.

articles.text: The shoulder pads and helmets are on for the Piedmont High football team as they get ready for the season opener on Friday, August 28 against Napa at Witter Field. The Highlanders return after reaching last year’s Division 7 North Coast Section Championship, but this year they have big positions to fill on offense and defense. Piedmont’s big changes start at the quarterback position after Jimmy Lagios transferred to Monte Vista. Head coach Jordan Seiden still hasn’t named the starter between sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson and junior Jonah Cha-Foster. He will get a better look at how each thrower handles live reps in their Saturday, August 22 scrimmage with Redwood Christian, Emerald, Weston Ranch, and Alameda. “This is the first time we won’t have a Lagios at the quarterback spot in five years. Cyrus has come so far, I can’t even quantify how far he’s developed. Jonah is an incredible athlete and might be our fastest player, Rehan Mumtaz included, who set the school record in the 100,” Seiden said. Emanuelson is making the step up from junior varsity and has been a consistent face at practice since the spring program opened up at the end of the 2026 school year. He’s been working with a quarterbacks coach, and has shown noticeable improvement with his delivery and poise. “When I got the news Jimmy was leaving, I started putting in a lot of work. At first, I didn’t have a lot of confidence and didn’t think I could compete at a varsity level. Over time, I started working with a coach and was getting a lot of support from my teammates. Now, my confidence is way up,” Emanuelson said. Cha-Foster is a much different type of quarterback as a dualthreat weapon. Although he had less time with the team due to his baseball schedule this summer, he has varsity experience as their primary backup last season and gives an added wrinkle to the offense with his running ability. “I’m just going day-by-day, keeping my head down, and looking to my teammates for support. I played baseball over the summer, but in between games I was throwing the football and studying the playbook, so I’m feeling prepared. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team returns after going 16-9 last season. They will host their first match in Piedmont since 2019. For the first time since 2019, Piedmont High will feature its water polo teams in town at the Piedmont Pool across the street from the school. It’s a hallmark moment for the team that has emerged as a perpetual contender in the Western Alameda County Conference and North Coast Section despite not having a pool at home. “It’s a joy to be back at the pool,” coach Rik Krumins said. “The facility is top notch, so Rylan Patty is back as a leading scorer from last season. we are all thrilled to be there. It feels like home base and it’s fun to interact with everyone there. It sort of feels like moving into a new apartment; we’re figuring out where everything is and where we all start to hang out.” During their time away from the Piedmont Pool, the high school won WACC title in 2022 and won the 2023 Division 2 North Coast Section title. Both of those teams never truly felt the love from a home crowd until their postseason runs, but now, Krumins is noticing how having a home pool gives them the attention they deserve. “It’s fun to see the guests show up. There were a bunch of kids at the little pool watching us practice, so hopefully there’s some organic water polo love going on there,” Krumins said. Last year’s squad finished its season with a 16-9 overall record and reached D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed while taking third place in the WACC Tournament. Although they bring back a young roster, they’ll be highlighted by important leading scorers and starters from last season like juniors Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, along with sophomore Ben Kappes. “We’re young. We have our juniors in Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, but after that it’s a sophomore heavy class. The goal is to develop everyone and within the next couple of years we’ll be back on top, that’s the goal,” Krumins said. Piedmont must replace at least two outfield players who graduated with the Class of 2026, including Elles Kreickhaus and Zach Dupree. Sophomore Walker Wilson got critical minutes as a freshman, while Krumins also highlighted sophomores Henry Van Den Bos and Graham Smith. “Walker Wilson played last year, he’ll play quite a bit. Graham Smith played club all summer long and has made tremendous strides. Henry Van Den Bos has been working really hard all summer. We’re throwing new ingredients in the pot and hoping it comes out positive,” Krumins said. As for the goalie role, Piedmont must fill in a critical spot held by three-year starter Luke McAuliffe. The Class of 2026 graduate was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after leading PHS to the 2023 D2 NCS title. Between the pipes will be another sophomore, Dylan Jerez, who Krumins says was a standout player in a preseason tournament they played in Hawaii. “Dylan Jerez is outstanding. He’s been playing club for three or four years. I took a team out to Hawaii in August and he shut people down. We placed third and a lot of that had to do with Dylan, he’s an outstanding goalie,” Krumins said. The PHS season starts on Monday, August 24 when visiting American High in Fremont. They play again on September 1 at Newark Memorial and will host their first match at the Piedmont Pool on Thursday, September 3. Henry Stein returns as a junior after being a leader in goals and assists last year.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team returns to Binks Rawlings Gym tomorrow, Thursday, August 20 against Berean Christian. The squad does so with a new head coach, Mike Glass, who took over the boys’ squad last season. Glass inherits a squad that looks poised for success in 2026. Last year’s team went 9-12 and accomplishing the school’s first berth in North Coast Section since 2018, falling in a five-set match to No. 9 Urban as the No. 8 seed in the opening round of the D4 bracket. The 2025 team featured eight sophomores and a freshman, all of which have returned to the varsity lineup. At outside hitter, juniors Maika Ting, Olivia Stevens, and Sofia Meyer return to the fold, as does three-year varsity senior Fiona Olsen. Ting was last year’s leader in kills, logging a gamehigh of 17 in 2025. “There’s a core set of juniors who are going to be stars for this team. Maika is clearly one of our leaders, and we’ll split time with Maika, Olivia Stevens, and Sofia Meyer. With Olivia, she’s been a starting libero, so this is a change in focus but she has all the right tools,” Glass said. PHS proved to be rich at the setter role last season with junior Allyson Huynh and freshman Carina Vora. Now in 2026, Huynh will be getting time at her natural libero role as Piedmont’s defensive leader, while Vora will continue at setter. Huynh earned an honorable mention for AllLeague honors as a sophomore last year. “Allyson is going to be a team leader. She’s been the team’s starting setter, but we are having her change to her natural position. She plays libero for club, we want her to do what she does best. We’re looking at three setters with Carina, Nora Trombi, and Mia Bechtel. All three of them Staff Photos Maika Ting returns as the team’s leader in kills last season. are neck-and-neck, so right now, they will be splitting the time and we’ll see who can develop as the season goes on,” Glass said. Along the middle, Glass is looking at juniors Lucia Dorsey and Izara Dando, along with freshman Charlotte Bailey. “We have Lucia, she has a lot of upside and is very athletic. She hits the ball hard. Izara Dando is also in the mix at middle and oppo, she’ll get looks at both. And then we have Charlotte Bailey, she’s 6 foot 3. As a freshman, asking her to be on the varsity squad means she has less experience but she loves volleyball; she’s already really good at volleyball, and can do a variety of things. We’re really excited about her,” Glass said. Glass comes with experience coaching the club level for the last five years, having spent time at Vibe Volleyball Club in Walnut Creek and Marin Volleyball Club in San Rafael. He also played collegiately on Rice’s club team. “I coached the boys’ varsity last year and was the assistant coach for the girls’ JV team last year. I’ve coached club volleyball for five seasons and have worked with everyone ages 9 to age 18. It’s just something that has become a big part of my life, I’m excited to help the Piedmont team and build the program,” Glass said. Olivia Stevens is another leading outside hitter back from last season. Third-year varsity junior Allyson Huynh moves from setter to libero.

articles.text: Center Repertory Company Artistic Director Matt Morrow Center Repertory Company launches its 2026-27 season with Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie, beginning Sunday, September 6 and running through Sunday, September 27. The 1944 semiautobiographical play follows a cast of characters in St. Louis: Tom Wingfield, an aspiring writer trapped in a warehouse job, supports his mother, Amanda, a former Southern belle, and his sister, Laura. Amanda, anxious about her daughter’s future, becomes determined to find her a romantic partner. Set against a backdrop of economic hardship and family tension in the 1930s, the play explores memory, desire, responsibility and the difficulty of escaping the past, and is an allnew production directed by Center Repertory Company Artistic Director Matt Morrow. “The Glass Menagerie was one of the first plays I read as an adolescent. Its heart-wrenching and poetic story made me fall in desperate love with the power of theatre,” Morrow said in a press release. “Four decades later, this exquisite masterpiece still haunts me, and I’m thrilled to launch my third season with Center Rep by directing it for the first time.” The cast includes Nancy Carlin, Alanna Darby, Rob Fagin, and Cody Sloan. The creative team includes Meg Neville as costume designer, Spense Matubang as lighting designer, Yi-Chien Lee as scenic designer and James Ard as sound designer. A “Director Chat” will be held before the September 11 performance at 6:30 p.m. A “Cast Chat” will be held September 23 following the performance. Performances are held at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center for the Arts beginning Sunday, September 6 and running through Sunday, September 27. For more information, visit centerrep.org.
articles.title: Center Rep presents The Glass Menagerie Sept. 6-27

articles.text: Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc features 75,000 hand-made bamboo kites. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) unveils Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc, the largest installation of Hashimoto’s career, with a public celebration tomorrow, Thursday, August 20. The art installation combines nearly 75,000 hand-made bamboo kites suspended together into a cloud canopy, covering the museum’s ground floor admission-free gallery from floor to ceiling and wall to wall. The unveiling will feature a conversation between the artist and SFMOMA Curator of Architecture and Design, Joseph Becker, as well as a sound performance by Nico Georis. “This giant arc of kites, color and pattern will be at once chaotic and meditative, playful and considered—a generous artwork that invites viewers to spend time in the gallery. It will be an enticing, intriguing overture to the museum itself,” said Hashimoto about the project. “Our mission at SFMOMA is radical hospitality for all—these efforts include filling over 45,000 square feet of free public space with irresistible contemporary art,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Hashimoto’s enveloping and breathtaking commission in our free-to-visit Roberts Family Gallery promises to welcome visitors of all ages, imbuing all who experience it with a sense of wonder and awe.” The event begins at 6 p.m. and admission is free. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ jacob-hashimoto-giant-arc/ to learn more.

articles.text: Project Hail Mary provides proof that a movie can be about averting doomsday while making time for laughs and real heart. Directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, based on the book by Andy Weir, Project Hail Mary stars Ryan Gosling as a scientist, Ryland Grace, who wakes up alone in space with no memory of how he got there. Ryland’s mission: figure out why the sun is dying and come up with a way to fix it before it’s too late. It’s a big task for one guy and a spaceship. Ryan Gosling carries this movie. A lot of the film is just him alone on a ship, and he makes that work through sheer performance, mixing humor with real desperation so you never lose interest even when it’s just one guy talking to himself. articles.text: August 12, 1839, was an important date in California history. On that day the pioneer John Sutter arrived at the confluence of the Sacramento and American Rivers to establish Sutter’s Fort, the founding, as it is generally reckoned, of California’s capital city, Sacramento. Accompanying Sutter were ten Hawaiians, three sailors, and one bulldog. One hundred eighty-seven years to the day later, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, another large party, 55 walkers and six K-9 best friends of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group, met at the Exedra to walk the caminos (streets) of Piedmont. Matt Gerhardt was the intrepid leader of the walkers last Wednesday. Intrigued by Piedmont’s streets with Spanish names, he decided to introduce them to his fellow walkers, every one of them, in fact, except Alta. Why not Alta? Because alta means “high” or “upper” in Spanish, and the group was reluctant to do that much uphill walking on a sunny summer day. With California history swirling through our heads, we marched from the Exedra, turned down Vista Avenue (vista, “view”), and headed north on Bonita Avenue (bonita, “pretty”) past the Frank C. Havens elementary school playground. It was the first week of school after summer vacation, and the children sounded happy and excited to be back. Crossing Oakland Avenue, we continued along Bonita, turned left on Blair Avenue toward Dracena Quarry Park, and then right on El Cerrito Avenue (“little hill”), which, as its name implied, was only the slightest of climbs. Dracena sounds as if it could be Spanish too (cena means “dinner”), but it is actually the name of a plant species, an appropriate name for Piedmont’s second-largest park. We took the group photo at the corner of El Cerrito and Ricardo Avenue, Ricardo being simply the Spanish for Richard, at the southwest corner of the park. Next the walkers traveled a short distance up Ricardo to a hidden passage connecting the street to York Drive below. Emerging from that green, shaded tunnel of shrubs, we continued down to Manor Drive and made a right turn to Arroyo Avenue (arroyo, “creek”). Then came another hidden passage, from Arroyo to Ramona Avenue, another Spanish given name. The walkers clambered down the stairway onto Ramona and turned uphill toward Estrella Avenue (estrella, “star”). We followed that leafy, treelined street until it ended at Moraga Avenue, and there we encountered a confluence of three Spanish-named streets: Bonita, Estrella, and Moraga. Not quite as momentous as Sutter reaching the meeting of the American and Sacramento Rivers 187 years ago, but still a pretty cool street sign, and “Bonita Estrella,” or Beautiful Star, would make a fine name for one of the Moraga family’s descendants. And what does moraga mean? It can be a bundle, like a bundle of harvested wheat, or, in southern Spain, a beach barbecue. But our street, like the town of Moraga over the hill, almost certainly honors a Californio family of the pre-Gold Rush Bay Area, and an interesting lot they were. The first Moraga in California was the patriarch, José Joaquín Moraga, second in command to General Juan Bautista de Anza in the Royal Spanish Army, who in 1776 became the comandante of San Francisco. His son Gabriel, also a soldier, traveled throughout Northern California and named many of its rivers, including the Sacramento, the very river beside which Sutter’s Fort would later rise. The town of Moraga was named for Gabriel’s son Joaquín, one of his fourteen children and the namesake of the original commander. Getting a good workout of our leg muscles, the walkers trudged up Moraga Avenue along what felt like a mountain trail to Monte Avenue (monte, fittingly, “mountain”), then climbed to Mesa Avenue, which, as its name promised, was flat as a table (mesa). Whew! From there it was all downhill on Pala Avenue to Highland. And at the corner of Pala and Highland we saw a man wielding a shovel, pala means exactly that, which gave us all a chuckle. Some of us will think of Pala as “Shovel Street” from now on. The walkers who remained after all those hills ambled back along Highland Avenue to the Exedra, where we thanked Matt for an excellent tour of the caminos of Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: Making recalls exciting and theatrical rather than repetitive obedience drills One of the most common dog training pain points for owners is recall. Whether it’s an emergency or not, your pup is always distracted along the way or seems to say, “Just a minute,” before responding—a minute that quickly turns into an eternity. The most essential part of recall training is the handler’s behavior and reactions. Below are some tips to increase your dog’s responsiveness and avoid common pitfalls that may be contributing to your dog’s unwillingness to come when called. The key to training your dog to move toward you without fail is to make it worth their while— in short, you have to get excited! Your dog has no reason to want to move your way unless you seem eager and interesting. Make sure your body language is inviting by bending over toward your dog. You can clap your hands or pat your thighs to seem even more encouraging. Always use a happy, high-pitched voice when calling your dog. If you are having trouble with this, squeal with delight as soon as your dog begins moving your way. This makes you much more interesting than any other distraction around and reinforces the dog’s recall with positive attention. When your dog gets to you, make sure you reward them right away. This can be with physical affection and praise or with treats. Remember that the reward must be given within three seconds of compliance. One common pitfall owners encounter is accidentally teaching the dog to associate coming when called with extra work. Avoid putting your dog through a predictable obedience routine, such as asking them to sit every time they get to you. After praising your dog, they should be dismissed to return to their play the majority of the time. Similarly, make sure that you are not leashing your dog and ending play every single time you call them. If your dog is giving you a hard time with recall, never reprimand A collie puppy comes running to her owner when called. the dog when they finally get to you. Even if your dog takes an eternity to complete their recall, ensure that compliance is met with praise each time—no matter how annoyed you are. While it is important to have a system in place that eventually teaches your dog that disregarding recall is not an option, reprimanding the dog when they finally comply gives mixed messages. Following these tips will not only improve your dog’s response but your relationship as well. One of the best parts of owning a dog is the unconditional excitement with which they greet you every day. By offering this in return whenever you call them, you will enrich your interactions with your furry friend and take irritation out of the equation. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Last year, Americans over 60 reported losing $7.7 billion to online criminals, a 59% jump in a single year, across more than 201,000 victims. The average loss was $38,500. More than 12,000 people lost over $100,000 each. And because federal researchers estimate that fewer than one in twenty victims ever reports the crime, the real number is far higher. These aren’t strangers in faraway places targeting careless people. They are targeting our parents, our neighbors, and increasingly, us. What’s changed: artificial intelligence. The “grandparent scam” used to rely on a panicked, muffled voice and a bad connection. Today, a scammer needs only a few seconds of audio, pulled from a Facebook video or a voicemail greeting, to clone your grandchild’s voice convincingly. The call comes at 11 p.m. There’s been an accident. Don’t tell Mom and Dad. Please hurry. THIS HAPPENED TO MY PARENTS. It’s real. To this day, my mom, Chase’s grandmother, is certain that the person calling was in fact Chase. It was not, but the voice sounded exactly like him. The FBI logged thousands of AI-related fraud complaints last year, with losses in the hundreds of millions. The technology is inexpensive, widely available, and improving monthly. The four that cost seniors the most: • Investment fraud. Now nearly half of all senior losses. Often begins as a friendly text “sent to the wrong number,” builds into a months-long relationship, then introduces a fake trading platform showing spectacular returns. The account balance is a screenshot. The money is gone. • Tech support scams. More than $1 billion lost last year. A pop-up or call claims to be Apple, Microsoft, or your bank and requests remote access to your computer. • Romance scams. Built patiently over weeks on Facebook, Instagram, or dating apps — then the emergency arrives. • Recovery scams. The cruelest category. Someone contacts a victim shortly after a loss, claims they can retrieve the stolen funds, and takes what’s left. A note for anyone buying or selling a home: wire fraud remains a serious threat in our industry. Criminals monitor transaction email and send fraudulent wiring instructions days before closing. Never wire funds based on emailed instructions. Call your escrow officer at a number you already have and verify verbally. Six habits that actually work: 1. Pause ten minutes. Urgency is the weapon. Every legitimate request survives a ten-minute delay. No scam does. 2. Hang up and call back on a number you already have — never the one provided to you. 3. Choose a family code word. A phrase only your family knows. Ask for it before you send anything. 4. Never grant remote access to your computer, and never send cryptocurrency to anyone you met online. Legitimate institutions do not ask you to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk. 5. Talk to someone before you act. Isolation is the scammer’s greatest ally. Seniors who call a family member first are dramatically less likely to lose money. 6. Report it — always. File at ic3.gov or call the Justice Department’s Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11. There is no shame in being targeted by a professional. Please forward this to your parents and children, friends and neighbors. Then call them, and talk it through. articles.text: There’s a persistent misconception that getting older means becoming less capable of learning something new. But in the performing arts, age can bring something else to the table: a lifetime of experiences to draw upon. Radhika Rao sees that firsthand teaching improv at Stagebridge in Oakland, the nation’s oldest performing arts organization for older adults. In fact, working with Stagebridge performers has changed the way Rao thinks about improv itself. “As we get older, our experiences get richer. We have all this backstory,” she says. Rather than emphasizing quick thinking or landing the cleverest line, Rao teaches for “presence of mind rather than speed or memory.” “You don’t have to chase the joke,” she says. “It’s about telling authentic stories, and the humor comes naturally.” Improv teacher Greg Philippi recently came to a similar conclusion after looking at aging, memory and long-form improv. “What matters more than memory is your ability to notice, associate, listen, and respond in the moment,” he wrote in The Armadillo Lab. Older improvisers, he Radhika Rao (center) and her students play 3 Headed Expert argues, have an advantage that’s easy to overlook: a much larger library of human experience. Research into creative aging suggests that participating in the arts may have benefits beyond the stage. The landmark Creativity and Aging Study, led by psychiatrist Gene Cohen, followed older adults participating in professionally led arts programs. Compared with a control group, participants reported better overall health, fewer doctor visits and greater social activity. But creativity as we age isn’t only about health. There’s something to be said for continuing to surprise ourselves with what we can learn and do. Stagebridge offers classes throughout the year, and this fall there are plenty of opportunities to do just that. Students can tell a story without words in Visual Comedy, dig into text and character in Monologues Through the Ages, or create stories for children using puppets and music. There’s also Shakespeare, songwriting, tap, musical theatre, folk dance and, of course, improv. Rao sees something else older adults bring to the stage. “As you get older, you stop worrying so much about what other people think,” she says. “My students bring that sort of permission to the stage.” Perhaps that’s a creative advantage worth celebrating. Stagebridge fall classes begin the week of Sept. 7 at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, across from Whole Foods near Lake Merritt. Need-based scholarships are available and class sizes are limited. Dear MacMama, My neighbor told me I should get a data wiper to remove my personal information from the internet. What is that, and can it help protect my identity and cut down on spam? – Angel, Oakland Dear Angel, I think your neighbor is talking about an automated personal data removal service. And though it provides some protection and can cut down on some spam it is not a fix-all. Let’s talk about what this kind of service is, what it does and what it doesn’t do. A personal data removal service can help protect your identity by scrubbing your personal details from data broker sites, and people search directories. The idea behind it is to reduce your digital footprint, which can cut down on targeted spam, and also lowers the risk of “doxxing” which is publishing someone’s private information online without their permission. They save you the trouble of contacting these data brokers and requesting that your information be scrubbed or erased. These services scan online public directories for your name, phone number and address and send requests to these brokers to delete your private files. Because in some cases this activity is automated, the services can do it much more quickly and efficiently than you can do it yourself. And they also will run regular scans because deleted data often returns. This can also reduce spam calls, text and junk mail, but it doesn’t eliminate them altogether. It also can remove your home address and family information from public search engines. These data removal services also continuously monitor these data brokers and request deletion automatically. Now for what they don’t do. They do not block hackers from stealing passwords or opening fake credit cards in your name. They also don’t erase things in public records like government registries, social media posts, and any court cases that have your name associated with them. They don’t replace the need for credit freezes, identity theft and dark web monitoring, and you still need to use very strong passwords or better yet passkeys. So, is it worth it to invest in one of these services? I personally am trying one to see if it reduces my spam. I already have credit monitoring and identity theft protection and have my credit frozen. If you decide to invest in one of these services, you will be asked to provide your legal name, address, phone number and email addresses. Most of them allow you to add at least one or two more email addresses. And most have a 30-day money back guarantee. Here are some highly rated companies, with some notable differences: 1. Incogni: (incogni.com). This is the one that I use. I have a family plan, for my husband and kids. This is $179 a year for one user. Incogni uses “set it and forget it” automation and covers 420+ brokers. 2. DeleteMe: ( joindeleteme. com) The cost for this is $129 a year for one user. This one uses human privacy experts to scrub personal information. This service requires a bit more oversight from users. 3. LifeLock by Norton: This is a very different service than the previous two. LifeLock monitors your credit, financial accounts and the dark web and offers insurance if your identity is compromised. LifeLock does not scan the web to remove your personal information and reduce your digital footprint but instead, works to protect you from the real-world consequences of stolen data. The plans start at a bit over $10 for the Core plan. By JoAnne Tobias There’s a persistent misconception that getting older means becoming less capable of learning something new. But in the performing arts, age can bring something else to the table: a lifetime of experiences to draw upon. Radhika Rao sees that firsthand teaching improv at Stagebridge in Oakland, the nation’s oldest performing arts organization for older adults. In fact, working with Stagebridge performers has changed the way Rao thinks about improv itself. “As we get older, our experiences get richer. We have all this backstory,” she says. Rather than emphasizing quick thinking or landing the cleverest line, Rao teaches for “presence of mind rather than speed or memory.” “You don’t have to chase the joke,” she says. “It’s about telling authentic stories, and the humor comes naturally.” Improv teacher Greg Philippi recently came to a similar conclusion after looking at aging, memory and long-form improv. “What matters more than memory is your ability to notice, associate, listen, and respond in the moment,” he wrote in The Armadillo Lab. Older improvisers, he Radhika Rao (center) and her students play 3 Headed Expert argues, have an advantage that’s easy to overlook: a much larger library of human experience. Research into creative aging suggests that participating in the arts may have benefits beyond the stage. The landmark Creativity and Aging Study, led by psychiatrist Gene Cohen, followed older adults participating in professionally led arts programs. Compared with a control group, participants reported better overall health, fewer doctor visits and greater social activity. But creativity as we age isn’t only about health. There’s something to be said for continuing to surprise ourselves with what we can learn and do. Stagebridge offers classes throughout the year, and this fall there are plenty of opportunities to do just that. Students can tell a story without words in Visual Comedy, dig into text and character in Monologues Through the Ages, or create stories for children using puppets and music. There’s also Shakespeare, songwriting, tap, musical theatre, folk dance and, of course, improv. Rao sees something else older adults bring to the stage. “As you get older, you stop worrying so much about what other people think,” she says. “My students bring that sort of permission to the stage.” Perhaps that’s a creative advantage worth celebrating. Stagebridge fall classes begin the week of Sept. 7 at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, across from Whole Foods near Lake Merritt. Need-based scholarships are available and class sizes are limited. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, My neighbor told me I should get a data wiper to remove my personal information from the internet. What is that, and can it help protect my identity and cut down on spam? – Angel, Oakland Dear Angel, I think your neighbor is talking about an automated personal data removal service. And though it provides some protection and can cut down on some spam it is not a fix-all. Let’s talk about what this kind of service is, what it does and what it doesn’t do. A personal data removal service can help protect your identity by scrubbing your personal details from data broker sites, and people search directories. The idea behind it is to reduce your digital footprint, which can cut down on targeted spam, and also lowers the risk of “doxxing” which is publishing someone’s private information online without their permission. They save you the trouble of contacting these data brokers and requesting that your information be scrubbed or erased. These services scan online public directories for your name, phone number and address and send requests to these brokers to delete your private files. Because in some cases this activity is automated, the services can do it much more quickly and efficiently than you can do it yourself. And they also will run regular scans because deleted data often returns. This can also reduce spam calls, text and junk mail, but it doesn’t eliminate them altogether. It also can remove your home address and family information from public search engines. These data removal services also continuously monitor these data brokers and request deletion automatically. Now for what they don’t do. They do not block hackers from stealing passwords or opening fake credit cards in your name. They also don’t erase things in public records like government registries, social media posts, and any court cases that have your name associated with them. They don’t replace the need for credit freezes, identity theft and dark web monitoring, and you still need to use very strong passwords or better yet passkeys. So, is it worth it to invest in one of these services? I personally am trying one to see if it reduces my spam. I already have credit monitoring and identity theft protection and have my credit frozen. If you decide to invest in one of these services, you will be asked to provide your legal name, address, phone number and email addresses. Most of them allow you to add at least one or two more email addresses. And most have a 30-day money back guarantee. Here are some highly rated companies, with some notable differences: 1. Incogni: (incogni.com). This is the one that I use. I have a family plan, for my husband and kids. This is $179 a year for one user. Incogni uses “set it and forget it” automation and covers 420+ brokers. 2. DeleteMe: ( joindeleteme. com) The cost for this is $129 a year for one user. This one uses human privacy experts to scrub personal information. This service requires a bit more oversight from users. 3. LifeLock by Norton: This is a very different service than the previous two. LifeLock monitors your credit, financial accounts and the dark web and offers insurance if your identity is compromised. LifeLock does not scan the web to remove your personal information and reduce your digital footprint but instead, works to protect you from the real-world consequences of stolen data. The plans start at a bit over $10 for the Core plan. Services like Incogni or DeleteMe and LifeLock can work well together: Incogni or DeleteMe reduces the amount of personal information available online, while LifeLock monitors for misuse. The average loss was $38,500. More than 12,000 people lost over $100,000 each. And because federal researchers estimate that fewer than one in twenty victims ever reports the crime, the real number is far higher. These aren’t strangers in faraway places targeting careless people. They are targeting our parents, our neighbors, and increasingly, us. What’s changed: artificial intelligence. The “grandparent scam” used to rely on a panicked, muffled voice and a bad connection. Today, a scammer needs only a few seconds of audio, pulled from a Facebook video or a voicemail greeting, to clone your grandchild’s voice convincingly. The call comes at 11 p.m. There’s been an accident. Don’t tell Mom and Dad. Please hurry. THIS HAPPENED TO MY PARENTS. It’s real. To this day, my mom, Chase’s grandmother, is certain that the person calling was in fact Chase. It was not, but the voice sounded exactly like him. The FBI logged thousands of AI-related fraud complaints last year, with losses in the hundreds of millions. The technology is inexpensive, widely available, and improving monthly. The four that cost seniors the most: • Investment fraud. Now nearly half of all senior losses. Often begins as a friendly text “sent to the wrong number,” builds into a months-long relationship, then introduces a fake trading platform showing spectacular returns. The account balance is a screenshot. The money is gone. • Tech support scams. More than $1 billion lost last year. A pop-up or call claims to be Apple, Microsoft, or your bank and requests remote access to your computer. • Romance scams. Built patiently over weeks on Facebook, Instagram, or dating apps — then the emergency arrives. • Recovery scams. The cruelest category. Someone contacts a victim shortly after a loss, claims they can retrieve the stolen funds, and takes what’s left. A note for anyone buying or selling a home: wire fraud remains a serious threat in our industry. Criminals monitor transaction email and send fraudulent wiring instructions days before closing. Never wire funds based on emailed instructions. Call your escrow officer at a number you already have and verify verbally. Six habits that actually work: 1. Pause ten minutes. Urgency is the weapon. Every legitimate request survives a ten-minute delay. No scam does. 2. Hang up and call back on a number you already have — never the one provided to you. 3. Choose a family code word. A phrase only your family knows. Ask for it before you send anything. 4. Never grant remote access to your computer, and never send cryptocurrency to anyone you met online. Legitimate institutions do not ask you to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk. 5. Talk to someone before you act. Isolation is the scammer’s greatest ally. Seniors who call a family member first are dramatically less likely to lose money. 6. Report it — always. File at ic3.gov or call the Justice Department’s Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11. There is no shame in being targeted by a professional. Please forward this to your parents and children, friends and neighbors. Then call them, and talk it through.
